title: Throughput & Latency debrief + routing decision - Corvina Systems POC
summary: Weekly pilot sync: reviewed this week's latency/throughput benchmarks vs Corvina's incumbent provider, identified tail-latency regressions under burst traffic, proposed routing + cache tweaks and request-level quantization to meet p95/p99 SLOs. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a targeted cold-start experiment, share updated routing playbook and revised cost projection; Corvina to enable trace flags and run an additional 2-hour traffic replay next Tue.
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-06-20 15:00 PT
- Duration: 48 minutes
- Recording id: ff-20250620-corvina-01

[00:00] Ethan Ramirez: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Ethan from Redwood here, I'll kick us off. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Mike Chen: Good, good. Morning for us. Thanks, Ethan. We got Sandra and Jeremy on as well.
[00:12] Priya Desai: Hi all, Priya from Redwood infra. Today we'll walk the benchmark deltas vs the incumbent and propose routing/quantization changes.
[00:20] Jeremy O'Neil: Quick note - we replayed Friday's peak window this morning per your ask, so we have that dataset ready.

[02:05] Ethan Ramirez: Okay jumping into the numbers. High level: p95 improved 12% over incumbent on steady traffic for the 2k token prompt set; p99 still shows a 25% regression under spikes. Priya, can you give the breakdown?
[02:20] Priya Desai: Sure. So baseline: incumbent is kind of optimized for long tail through batching heuristics - they were doing bigger micro-batches for 99th. Our steady-state throughput is better because of continuous batching and smaller per-request HT, but when we hit concurrent bursts we observed more KV cache misses — spelled out in the logs as "kv cash miss" in the proto logs so some of the auto parser garbled that — and cold-start kernel warmup costs spiked. That added ~80-160ms to some requests, which pushed the p99 up.
[03:10] Sandra Lopez: Is that the same as the warming penalty we saw earlier in the pilot? We thought the slot sizing might be too small.
[03:18] Priya Desai: Partly. There's a couple of contributors: cold kv-cache population, then the first few attention kernels after quantized fallback have higher latency — we think there are two things: one, our kernel dispatch for the int8 path is still hitting a slower codegen hot path on these particular sequences; two, the request patterns cause some interleaving that prevents ideal batching.

[04:45] Mike Chen: Numbers wise, at 150 qps sustained you're fine, but at 450 qps burst p99 goes from 420ms (incumbent) to about 560ms on Redwood, right?
[04:54] Priya Desai: Roughly yes, that's what we saw in the replay. The median and p95 remain better at 150-300 qps.

[06:10] Ethan Ramirez: Important to stress the tail regressions only occur under the burst profile. For Corvina's success criteria you defined p95 < 300ms and p99 < 650ms for your core inference flow. We're inside p95 but p99 is close to the threshold.
[06:25] Sandra Lopez: We hit p95 consistently; p99 occasionally crosses 650ms during traffic spikes. That was our red line.

[07:40] Priya Desai: Proposed mitigations we tested locally: 1) aggressive prefix caching so KV hits are higher; 2) increase reserved slot count during predicted peak windows to reduce cold starts; 3) request-level quantization toggles: keep fp16 for the first N tokens then switch to int8 for the remainder to avoid initial kernel slow-paths; 4) routing policy: route burst traffic to a slightly higher-cost but warmed pool (dedicated slots) and keep background steady-state on cheaper shared.

[09:30] Jeremy O'Neil: That hybrid routing idea could work, but we need clarity on cost delta and how quickly Redwood can scale up reserved slots on short notice.
[09:38] Ethan Ramirez: For dedicated slots we can provision warm buffers, but there's a ramp of about 5-10 minutes to get fully warmed depending on model and quant profile. This is why pre-warmed pools + predictive autoscale for known windows is a safer bet.

[11:55] Mike Chen: About quality: when you toggle quantization mid-request, any risk of output drift? We have regulatory checks so any quality drop is a blocker.
[12:04] Priya Desai: Good question. The mid-request approach we tested keeps the seed generation in fp16 for the first 64 tokens (your prompts are often long) then switches to int8 for the tail. In our head-to-head with your eval set we saw negligible BLEU/ROUGE change and human spot checks showed no meaningful degradation, but we flagged some edge cases with factual hallucination in very long context windows. We recommend running your regression suite against a canary before enabling globally.

[15:00] Ethan Ramirez: Ok, let's walk the specific experiments. Priya, do you want to call out the three runs we agreed to spin up?
[15:07] Priya Desai: Yep. Run A: cold-start focus — we will intentionally tear down cache and measure kernel warmup times across three slot sizes. Run B: hybrid routing simulation — route 30% of burst traffic to pre-warmed reserved pool while rest goes to shared. Run C: mid-request quantization canary against your eval prompt set with telemetry on quality metrics. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, token throughput, and request-level quality markers.

[18:20] Sandra Lopez: Timing? Can Run C be done with the replay we have this week? We can also flip on the debug trace flags to capture per-token latencies.
[18:30] Priya Desai: Yes, Run C can consume your replay. Run A and B we'd like to run during a maintenance window so we don't interfere with real traffic.

[20:40] Mike Chen: One other operational ask: we need audit logs for model routing decisions and per-request traces to debug when fallbacks happen. Does Redwood provide that?
[20:50] Ethan Ramirez: Yes—Console exports include per-route traces and token-level cost and latency breakdowns. We can grant Corvina a read-only view scoped to the pilot resources and we'll email the short doc for enabling extended retention.

[23:05] Jeremy O'Neil: On cost - what's the estimated unit cost for the hybrid routing run vs incumbent? We don't want runaway $/req during burst windows.
[23:14] Ethan Ramirez: Early estimate: hybrid routing at current pilot configuration increases instance cost for the bursted portion by ~18-25% vs fully shared. But because p50/p95 are better and we avoid SLA penalties, net cost per successful inference may be similar or lower. We'll run a cost projection spreadsheet and share.

[26:40] Priya Desai: We also found a small tuning knob in the runtime: reducing the per-worker maximum batch size in the shared pool for the specific model reduces queueing jitter under mixed-length requests. It slightly lowers throughput but tightens p99. Might be worth a tradeoff.

[29:55] Sandra Lopez: If we lower batches, how much throughput do we lose? Our throughput target is 10k tokens/s for the service.
[30:05] Priya Desai: For the replay profile, it reduced token throughput by roughly 6% but improved p99 by ~18% in the shared pool. For your overall budget we'd expect this to be acceptable if burst windows are mitigated by reserved slots.

[33:10] Mike Chen: Any security concerns with the pre-warmed reserved pool? We need to make sure data never leaves our tenant boundary.
[33:18] Ethan Ramirez: Dedicated slots are tenant-isolated; data plane stays within your VPC for Redwood Private and dedicated pools. We can provide the SOC2 and network diagrams. For hosted pilot, we ensure encryption at rest and in transit and can push logs to your SIEM.

[36:00] Priya Desai: One small catch: when we toggled the mid-request quantization in our internal canary, one prompt pattern with many short instructions created slightly different tokenization which affected a downstream parser in your pipeline — likely minor but worth running the full regression.

[38:50] Jeremy O'Neil: Understood. We'll run that parser in our replay.

[40:15] Ethan Ramirez: Let's summarize actions and owners. Also note, competitor behaviors: incumbent seems to batch more aggressively and accept higher median latency to keep tail lower; another vendor you mentioned, TritonServe, has similar batching heuristics but less dynamic routing.

[41:05] Priya Desai: Quick recap of agreement: Redwood runs Runs A/B/C, shares results and cost projections by Friday, Corvina runs one additional 2-hour replay with trace flags next Tue, then we'll reconvene to make a routing decision.

[43:30] Mike Chen: Sounds good. If the canary passes, we're comfortable with a phased roll where reserved slots cover nightly peaks and we monitor for 48 hours.

[45:00] Ethan Ramirez: Great. Anything else?
[45:06] Sandra Lopez: One last ask — can you add a small section in the playbook about trace IDs and how to correlate with our logs? That'll speed triage.
[45:14] Ethan Ramirez: Yep we'll add it.

[46:00] Ethan Ramirez: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the experiment plan and spreadsheet. Talk soon.
[47:30] Meeting end

Corvina to enable debug trace flags and run 2-hour traffic replay on 2025-06-24 and share logs
